title: Special mercy object: antecedent remitted vs to-be-remitted (Cassander/Cologne)
source_text: LVI. Proinde id solum hic videtur controverti, An misericordia Dei specialis pertineat ad fidei justificantis objectum, & sit ejus praecipua pars? quod Protestantes communiter affirmant, negant vero Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae. Verum hic observandum est misericordiam illam specialem dupliciter considerari posse, ut jam superioribus Thesibus ostendimus, nempe, vel ut gratiam quandam antecedentem, & quam ille qui credit jam adeptus est, veluti quum quis credit sibi jam esse remissa peccata; vel ut aliquid per fidem obtinendum, veluti quum credimus peccata nobis esse remittenda. Et videntur quidem ex Reformatis nonnulli actus illius fidei per quem justificamur objectum constituere misericordiam quandam specialem antecedentem, quasi justificaremur per actum illum fidei quo certo statuimus peccata per Christum nobis esse remissa. Qua in re quoque nonnullos ex Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae astipulantes habent, sicut patet ex iis quae supra de Theologis Coloniensibus ex Georgio Cassandro relata sunt. Sed Theologi Reformati complures, non misericordiam quandam antecedentem, sed quam fidelis a Deo se consecuturum confidit, illius fidei actus per quem justificamur objectum constituunt. Neque dicunt nos justificari per fidem qua credimus peccata nobis jam esse remissa, sed qua credimus peccata per Christum esse remittenda.
pass_a_gloss: Accordingly the only thing that seems controverted here is whether God special mercy belongs to the object of justifying faith and is its principal part — which Protestants commonly affirm and the Doctors of the Roman Church deny. But here it must be observed that that special mercy can be considered in two ways, as we already showed in earlier theses: either as a certain antecedent grace which the one who believes has already obtained, as when someone believes his sins are already remitted to him; or as something to be obtained through faith, as when we believe sins are to be remitted to us. And indeed some of the Reformed seem to make the object of that faith-act by which we are justified a certain special antecedent mercy, as if we were justified by that faith-act by which we certainly establish that sins have been remitted to us through Christ. In which matter they also have some Roman Doctors agreeing, as is clear from what was related above about the Cologne theologians from Georg Cassander. But many Reformed theologians make the object of that faith-act by which we are justified not a certain antecedent mercy but that which the believer trusts he will obtain from God. Nor do they say we are justified by the faith by which we believe sins are already remitted to us, but by that by which we believe sins are to be remitted through Christ.
pass_b_english: The live fight is whether special mercy is justifying faith object and chief part — Protestants usually yes, Rome no.

Special mercy may be antecedent (already remitted) or still to be obtained; some Reformed and even Cologne/Cassander treat antecedent remitted-sins persuasion as justifying, but many Reformed put to-be-remitted trust as the justifying object.

lemmas.gloss: sins are to be remitted through Christ

choices.why: Antecedent vs to-be-obtained splits the object fight.
